Slaughter
slaw'ter
n. (killing, especially of animals or in great numbers; rendering Hebrew tebach, Greek sphage)
From the Saxon slaht, from slean, to slay — the same root as slay and slew. Hebrew tebach is a butchering, the killing of an animal for food or sacrifice, so the word carries the atmosphere of the shambles rather than of the battlefield.

Biblical Definition

Slaughter is butchering, and Scripture's central use of it is the silence of the Servant: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). It is the passage the Ethiopian eunuch was reading when Philip joined his chariot, and it is the plainest Old Testament statement that the Messiah would be killed as a sacrificial animal is killed — without resistance and without protest. Proverbs uses the same figure for the young man walking into sin without any idea what is happening to him: “He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks” (Proverbs 7:22) — the beast walks calmly because it does not know the destination. Jeremiah asks God to deal with the prosperous wicked in these terms: “pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter” (Jeremiah 12:3). And Paul quotes the Psalter to describe the church's ordinary condition: “we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Romans 8:36) — immediately before saying we are more than conquerors.

Webster 1828 Definition

Butchering; killing as of animals. Scripture's chief use is Isaiah 53:7, the Servant brought as a lamb to the slaughter and opening not his mouth — and the church accounted as sheep for the slaughter.

expand to see more

SLAUGHTER, n. slaw'ter. [Sax. slaht, from slean, to slay.] A killing; destruction of life by violence.

2. The killing of oxen or other beasts for market; butchery.

3. Great destruction of life by violence; carnage; as, a great slaughter in battle.

4. In Scripture, of the Servant; as, he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, Isa. 53.

5. Of the church's affliction; as, we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter, Rom. 8.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 53:7 — "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth."

Proverbs 7:22 — "He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks;"

Romans 8:36 — "As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter."

Jeremiah 12:3 — "But thou, O LORD, knowest me: thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart toward thee: pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter."

Modern Corruption

The cross is recast as tragedy, miscarriage of justice, or moral demonstration. Isaiah's image is a sacrificial animal led to the block — deliberate, appointed, and silently accepted.

expand to see more

Every attempt to make the crucifixion something other than a sacrifice must get past Isaiah 53:7, and past Philip's use of it. The eunuch asked whether the prophet spoke of himself or of some other man, and Philip began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus. The imagery is not of a hero cut down or of a martyr making a point; it is of a lamb going to the block. The silence matters too: he opened not his mouth. He was not overpowered, and he did not protest, because the death was the errand.

The principle to recover is what Romans 8:36 does with the same figure. Paul applies the slaughter language to the church — killed all the day long, accounted as sheep for the slaughter — and then, without changing the subject, says that in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. Christian victory is not the avoidance of the slaughter but conquest through it, on the pattern of the Lamb. Proverbs 7:22 supplies the sober warning about a different procession: the man walking into sin is also going to a slaughter, and calmly, because he cannot see the end of the road.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tebach is a butchering or slaughter, from tabach, to slay an animal. Greek sphage is slaughter, from sphazo, the verb used of the Lamb slain in Revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew tebach (H2874) — a butchering, a slaughter; as a lamb to the slaughter.

Hebrew tabach (H2873) — to slay, to butcher; the verb of the shambles.

Hebrew hereg (H2027) — killing, slaughter; the day of the great slaughter in Isaiah 30.

Greek sphage (G4967) — slaughter; sheep for the slaughter, Romans 8:36.

Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay sacrificially; the Lamb as it had been slain, Revelation 5:6.

Usage

"Of the silent Servant: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7)."

"Of the young man walking into sin: as an ox goeth to the slaughter (Proverbs 7:22)."

"Of the church's ordinary condition: we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter (Romans 8:36)."
